snapshot.opening_post:
You don't need long context!

NVIDIA researchers just published a paper questioning whether LLMs actually need huge context windows for long-running tasks.

The problem is that longer context is expensive.

As the context grows, every new token gets slower to generate, uses more memory, and costs more to serve.

In their measurements, going from a 16K to 256K context increased the cost per generated token by 3.6× for GLM 5.2, 5.6× for Kimi K2.6, and 7× for Qwen 3 Coder Next.

Their alternative is frequent context compaction.

Instead of carrying the entire conversation history through a long agent run, you keep a compact representation of the current task state and start a new context when needed.

For long documents, they use a similar idea: keep the documents outside the context and let the agent selectively read the parts it needs rather than loading everything at once.

They test this across software engineering, terminal tasks, tool use, retrieval, and long-document reasoning.

And the results are pretty interesting.

On long-horizon tasks, frequent compaction generally maintained or even improved task accuracy compared with keeping the full history.

They pushed this even further with Single-Action Compaction.

The model takes one action, observes the result, updates a compact semantic state, and then the entire conversation is discarded before the next action.

On Claude Opus 4.5, this preserved SWE-bench Verified performance and improved Terminal-Bench.

On GPT 5.6 Sol, the accuracy drop was only a few percentage points, while the median peak live context stayed around 7–9K tokens.

The paper takes this idea further and proposes Semantic State Space Models.

Instead of maintaining an ever-growing conversation history, the model carries a compact natural-language state between turns containing the information needed to continue the task.

This feels especially relevant for long-running agents.

You may not need to keep hundreds of thousands of tokens alive throughout the entire run. Keep the current state, retrieve what you need, compact aggressively, and continue.

I've shared the paper below!

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05306

snapshot.opening_post:
My favorite Claude Code tip lately: set auto-compact to 400k

By default, Claude Code lets a conversation grow to about 967k tokens before it compacts, so I moved mine to 400k.

Models tend to get worse at recalling details as the context window fills up (people call it context rot), and Anthropic writes about it in their own context engineering guide.

So when I run long tasks or goals, Claude compacts well before it gets anywhere near that territory.

I've been letting goals run for hours like this and getting noticeably better results.

The tradeoff is more compactions, but for long goals it's been worth it for me.

It also goes a little easier on my usage limits, since every turn isn't re-reading a nearly full context window.

How to set it:
→ Type /autocompact in Claude Code and pick a window
→ Or add "autoCompactWindow": 400000 to your settings.json (you can also just ask Claude to do this in natural language)

snapshot.opening_post:
Spent some time reading through Google's Antigravity /teamwork docs. Honestly, they nailed a lot of hard stuff here. Upfront scoping, isolated folders, exclusive file ownership, plus Critic, Challenger, and Auditor roles actually trying to break the code before it ships.

The part I'm stealing for my own setup is how they handle context rot. After every milestone, the Project Orchestrator hands structured plan and progress files to a fresh instance instead of dragging one bloated chat for hours.

Where I'd do it differently is the final gate. Having an LLM Auditor check terminal output catches lazy mistakes, sure, but it's still a model grading another model.

In my own code (screenshot), the final check is completely offline and deterministic. Known receipt schemas only, raw byte hashing tied to the workspace fingerprint, networkRequests: 0, hard GO or NO_GO. Every return path also forces authorizationGranted: false and only outputs the nextAllowedAction.

An agent can't sweet-talk its way past a hash check, and passing verification never quietly turns into permission to run stuff.

top_replies.author: @JiaShen_AI
top_replies.text:
"Passing verification never quietly turns into permission" is the line I'd frame. We hit exactly that in our own runs: a frozen package is not a go signal, and the run needs a separate, explicit yes.

One layer I'd add: a hash check proves the bytes are the ones you froze. It can't tell you the thing you froze measures what you think it measures. Reproducible and correct are two different gates, and the second one still needs a human looking at what the numbers mean.

top_replies.text: True, the hash just stops the agent from faking what ran. Still need eyes on whether the metric makes sense.

snapshot.opening_post:
your CLAUDE.md is a wish list

the agent reads it, weighs it, and skips it at step 40

hooks don't ask. they check

6 events, 3 exit codes and the Stop hook that makes "done" mean the tests passed https://x.com/i/article/2124419087090823168

You wrote "never run rm -rf" in CLAUDE.md. Forty steps later the agent ran it anyway
Not because it ignored you. Because a line in context is a request, and requests get weighed against everything else the model is holding
Getting out of that loop takes one idea most people never set up: a hook
A rule asks the model to behave. A hook checks whether it did, and stops the action when it didn't
Here is the split, the six events that matter, the three ways a hook answers, and the one hook that ends "I'm done" without tests

A rule is a request, a hook is a check
CLAUDE.md is loaded into context and read by the model. That is its strength and its ceiling
It is great for guidance: how the project is laid out, which commands to use, what style the team likes
It cannot fail an action. If the model decides step 40 is the exception, nothing stops it
A hook is different in kind. It is a command bound to an event in Claude Code's lifecycle, and it runs every time that event fires
The model does not need to remember it, agree with it, or even know it exists
So the sorting rule is simple. If breaking it is annoying, keep it in CLAUDE.md. If breaking it is expensive, move it into a hook

Where hooks live
Hooks sit in your settings files: .claude/settings.json for the project, ~/.claude/settings.json for you everywhere
Each one names an event, an optional matcher for which tool it applies to, and what to run:

The hook gets the event as JSON on stdin: the tool name, the tool input, the session, the working directory
That is all the context it needs. It reads the input, decides, and answers

Six events to learn first
There are more events than six, but these carry almost every useful setup
SessionStart runs when a session starts, resumes, clears or compacts. Use it to load live context: open issues, the current branch, what changed overnight
UserPromptSubmit runs before Claude sees your message. It can add context to every prompt, or reject one outright
PreToolUse runs before a tool call and is the only gate in front of it. It can allow, ask, or deny
PostToolUse runs after a tool returns. The action already happened, so this is where you format, lint and log
Stop runs when Claude is about to finish. Block it and Claude keeps working
PreCompact runs before context is trimmed. Write down anything you will want after it shrinks
Two of these do most of the work. PreToolUse guards the call. Stop guards the word "done"

A hook has three ways to answer
Everything else is detail

Exit 0 with nothing printed means no decision. The normal permission flow applies, and the hook was just watching
Exit 2 means block. The action stops, and whatever the hook printed to stderr goes back to Claude as the reason
This is the whole rm guard:

The stderr line matters more than it looks. A bare refusal makes the agent try a variation. A refusal with an alternative makes it switch
Exit 0 with JSON is the precise version. On PreToolUse you return a permission decision and a reason:

"deny" cancels the call and tells Claude why. "ask" shows you the normal prompt. "allow" skips the prompt, though your deny rules still apply
Pick one style per hook. Exit 2 or JSON, not both

The hook nobody writes: Stop
Every agent says "done". Very few are made to prove it
A Stop hook runs at the exact moment Claude is about to hand the turn back. Return decision: "block" with a reason, and instead of stopping, Claude reads the reason and keeps going
Put your test suite there and "done" stops being a claim

Two brakes keep this from looping forever, and both are built in
stop_hook_active is true when Claude is already continuing because of a stop hook. Check it, or a test that can never pass will hold the session hostage
And after eight continuations in a row, Claude Code ends the turn anyway
The reason field is the part to get right. Send the failing test and the last lines of output, not "tests failed". The agent fixes what it can see

Five kinds of hook, and four of them are not a model

command runs a script. It is the cheapest, the fastest, and the only one that gives the same answer every time
http posts the same JSON to a URL, so one server can enforce one policy across a whole team
mcp_tool calls a tool from a server you already connected
prompt sends the input to a model for a single judgment, returned as JSON
agent spawns a subagent that can read files and search before it decides. It is the slowest and still marked experimental
The test for which one you need: if you can describe the rule without the words judge, assess or decide, it is a command hook
"No writes outside src/" is a command. "Does this change match the ticket?" is a prompt
A setup where every check is a model call pays for judgment on questions that had one correct answer

Where to start on your own setup
Take the rule you repeat most often in chat. The one you type for the third time this week
Write it as a PreToolUse command hook that exits 2 with an alternative in stderr
Then add one Stop hook that runs your fastest check: lint, types, or the tests for the files that changed
Then one PostToolUse formatter, so you never review whitespace again
Leave prompt and agent hooks for last, and only for rules a script cannot state
Put the human where the hooks can't reach: the merge, the deploy, the migration
Three lines hold the whole discipline
A rule the model can skip is a suggestion
A check that can't fail is decoration
And every correction you type twice belongs in a hook
